UNITS.title: Angles, triangles and the unit circle
Graphs, identities, inverses and the triangle laws

SECTIONS.title: Angles, degrees and radians
ideas: An angle in standard position starts on the positive $x$-axis; positive angles turn counterclockwise, negative angles clockwise.
A radian is the angle that cuts off an arc as long as the radius. A full turn is $2\pi$ radians, so $360^\circ = 2\pi$ and $180^\circ = \pi$.

To convert, multiply by $\frac{\pi}{180^\circ}$ (degrees to radians) or $\frac{180^\circ}{\pi}$ (radians to degrees). Memorize the landmarks: $30^\circ = \frac\pi6$, $45^\circ = \frac\pi4$, $60^\circ = \frac\pi3$, $90^\circ = \frac\pi2$.
Coterminal angles share a terminal side: add or subtract $360^\circ$ (or $2\pi$) as many times as you like.
With $\theta$ in radians: arc length $s = r\theta$, sector area $A = \frac12r^2\theta$, and linear speed $v = r\omega$ for angular speed $\omega$.

example.p: Convert $150^\circ$ to radians and find the arc it cuts off on a circle of radius 4.

pitfalls: Using degrees in $s = r\theta$; it needs radians.
Converting the wrong way: multiplying degrees by $\frac{180}{\pi}$.
SECTIONS.tip: Think of $\pi$ as $180^\circ$: then $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ is $5\cdot30^\circ = 150^\circ$ at a glance.

SECTIONS.title: Right triangle trigonometry and similar triangles
ideas: For an acute angle $\theta$ in a right triangle: $\sin\theta = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\cos\theta = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$, $\tan\theta = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}$ (SOH CAH TOA).
Similar triangles have the same angles, so their sides are proportional. That is why the ratios depend only on the angle, not on the size of the triangle, and why you can find heights from shadows.
The special triangles: $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ has sides $1 : 1 : \sqrt2$; $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ has sides $1 : \sqrt3 : 2$ (short leg opposite $30^\circ$).
Cofunctions: $\sin\theta = \cos(90^\circ-\theta)$, because the two acute angles of a right triangle share the same sides.
Angles of elevation (looking up) and depression (looking down) turn real situations into right triangles: height $=$ distance $\times\tan(\text{angle})$.

example.p: From 50 ft away, the angle of elevation to the top of a tree is $30^\circ$. How tall is the tree?

pitfalls: Mixing up opposite and adjacent: they depend on which angle you are using.
Putting the $\sqrt3$ on the wrong leg of the $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle: the longer leg is opposite $60^\circ$.
SECTIONS.tip: Draw both special triangles in the margin at the start of every exam.

SECTIONS.title: The unit circle
ideas: On the unit circle (radius 1), the angle $t$ lands at the point $(\cos t, \sin t)$. This defines sine and cosine for every angle, not just acute ones.
Since $x^2+y^2 = 1$: $\sin^2t+\cos^2t = 1$, and both $\sin t$ and $\cos t$ lie between $-1$ and $1$.

First-quadrant values: at $\frac\pi6$ the point is $\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac12\right)$; at $\frac\pi4$, $\left(\frac{\sqrt2}2,\frac{\sqrt2}2\right)$; at $\frac\pi3$, $\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$.
The reference angle is the acute angle to the $x$-axis. Every other angle's values are the reference angle's values with signs set by the quadrant.
Signs by quadrant: I all positive; II sine positive; III tangent positive; IV cosine positive ("All Students Take Calculus").

example.s: $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ is in quadrant II with reference angle $\frac\pi6$. So $\sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac12$ (positive in II) and $\cos\frac{5\pi}{6} = -\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

pitfalls: Swapping $\sin$ and $\cos$: cosine is the $x$-coordinate, sine the $y$.
Forgetting the sign from the quadrant.
SECTIONS.tip: Memorize only the first quadrant. Every other value is a reference angle plus a sign.

SECTIONS.title: The other trigonometric functions
ideas: $\tan t = \frac{\sin t}{\cos t}$, $\sec t = \frac{1}{\cos t}$, $\csc t = \frac{1}{\sin t}$ and $\cot t = \frac{\cos t}{\sin t}$. Each is undefined where its denominator is 0, such as $\tan\frac\pi2$.
Even and odd: cosine and secant are even, $\cos(-t) = \cos t$. Sine, cosecant, tangent and cotangent are odd, $\sin(-t) = -\sin t$.
More Pythagorean identities: divide $\sin^2t+\cos^2t = 1$ by $\cos^2t$ to get $1+\tan^2t = \sec^2t$, or by $\sin^2t$ to get $1+\cot^2t = \csc^2t$.
Sine and cosine repeat every $2\pi$; tangent and cotangent repeat every $\pi$.
Given one value and the quadrant, find the rest by drawing a reference triangle and attaching signs.

formulas.t: \tan t=\frac{\sin t}{\cos t},\ \sec t=\frac1{\cos t},\ \csc t=\frac1{\sin t},\ \cot t=\frac{\cos t}{\sin t}

example.p: If $\sin t = \frac35$ and $t$ is in quadrant II, find $\cos t$, $\tan t$ and $\sec t$.
example.s: Reference triangle 3-4-5. In quadrant II cosine is negative: $\cos t = -\frac45$, $\tan t = \frac{3/5}{-4/5} = -\frac34$, $\sec t = -\frac54$.

pitfalls: Thinking $\sec t = \frac{1}{\sin t}$; secant goes with cosine, cosecant with sine.
Dropping the sign when finding the missing side of the reference triangle.
SECTIONS.tip: "Co" pairs with "non-co": secant with cosine, cosecant with sine.

SECTIONS.title: Graphs of sine and cosine
ideas: $y = \sin x$ starts at 0, rises to 1 at $\frac\pi2$, returns to 0 at $\pi$, falls to $-1$ at $\frac{3\pi}2$ and is back at 0 at $2\pi$. $y = \cos x$ is the same wave shifted left by $\frac\pi2$: it starts at its maximum.
Sine is odd: its graph is symmetric about the origin. Cosine is even: its graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis.
For $y = A\sin\big(B(x-C)\big)+D$: amplitude $|A|$, period $\frac{2\pi}{|B|}$, phase shift $C$ (right if positive), midline $y = D$.
The maximum is $D+|A|$ and the minimum $D-|A|$, so the range is $[D-|A|,\ D+|A|]$.
To sketch one period, split it into four equal parts and plot the five key points: midline, max, midline, min, midline (for sine).

example.s: Amplitude 3, period $\frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi$, midline $y = -1$, range $[-4, 2]$. It starts at its maximum, $2$, at $x = 0$.

pitfalls: Reading the phase shift from $\sin(2x-\pi)$ as $\pi$; factor first: $\sin\big(2(x-\frac\pi2)\big)$ shifts by $\frac\pi2$.
Using $B$ as the period instead of $\frac{2\pi}{B}$.
SECTIONS.tip: Find the midline and amplitude first, then the period; the sketch follows.

SECTIONS.title: Inverse trigonometric functions
ideas: Trig functions repeat, so they are not one-to-one. Their inverses use restricted domains, and each returns one angle.

$\arcsin x$ (or $\sin^{-1}x$) takes $x\in[-1,1]$ and returns an angle in $\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]$. $\arccos x$ returns an angle in $[0,\pi]$. $\arctan x$ takes any $x$ and returns an angle in $\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$.
$\sin(\arcsin x) = x$ for $x$ in $[-1,1]$, but $\arcsin(\sin x) = x$ only when $x$ is in $\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]$: $\arcsin\left(\sin\frac{5\pi}6\right) = \frac\pi6$.
For expressions like $\cos(\arcsin\frac35)$, draw the triangle for the inner angle and read off the outer function.
To solve $\sin x = \frac12$ on $[0,2\pi)$, find the reference angle $\frac\pi6$ and every quadrant where sine is positive: $x = \frac\pi6$ or $\frac{5\pi}6$.

example.s: $\arccos$ returns an angle in $[0,\pi]$ with cosine $-\frac12$: $\frac{2\pi}3$. For the second, $\arcsin\frac35$ is an angle with opposite 3 and hypotenuse 5, so adjacent 4 and the cosine is $\frac45$.

pitfalls: Reading $\sin^{-1}x$ as $\frac{1}{\sin x}$; that is $\csc x$.
SECTIONS.tip: Memorize each range as a picture: arcsin and arctan live on the right half of the circle, arccos on the top half.

SECTIONS.title: Verifying identities
ideas: An identity is true for every value where both sides are defined. To verify one, transform one side until it matches the other; never work on both sides at once as if it were an equation.
Toolkit: reciprocal and quotient identities, the Pythagorean identities $\sin^2+\cos^2 = 1$, $1+\tan^2 = \sec^2$, $1+\cot^2 = \csc^2$, and even and odd identities.
Strategies: start with the more complicated side; rewrite everything in sines and cosines; combine fractions over a common denominator; factor; multiply by a conjugate like $1+\cos x$.
Simplifying is the same skill: $\frac{1-\cos^2x}{\sin x} = \frac{\sin^2x}{\sin x} = \sin x$.
pitfalls: Cross-multiplying or adding to both sides, which assumes what you are trying to prove.
SECTIONS.tip: When stuck, convert to sines and cosines; it nearly always opens a path.

SECTIONS.title: Sum, difference and double-angle formulas
ideas: $\sin(\alpha\pm\beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta\pm\cos\alpha\sin\beta$.
$\cos(\alpha\pm\beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta\mp\sin\alpha\sin\beta$: note the sign flips.
They give exact values for angles like $15^\circ = 45^\circ-30^\circ$ and $75^\circ = 45^\circ+30^\circ$.
Double angle: $\sin2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $\cos2\theta = \cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta = 1-2\sin^2\theta = 2\cos^2\theta-1$.
To use them you need both the sine and cosine of each angle: find the missing one from a reference triangle and the quadrant.
pitfalls: Keeping the plus sign in the cosine sum formula; it becomes a minus.
SECTIONS.tip: Check an exact answer with a calculator at home: $\cos75^\circ\approx0.2588$.

SECTIONS.title: The Laws of Sines and Cosines
ideas: They solve triangles that are not right triangles. Label sides $a, b, c$ opposite angles $A, B, C$.
Law of Sines: $\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C}$. Use it when you know a side and its opposite angle (AAS, ASA, or SSA).
SSA is the ambiguous case: there may be no triangle, one, or two, because $\sin B = k$ has two solutions between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$.
Law of Cosines: $c^2 = a^2+b^2-2ab\cos C$. Use it for two sides and the angle between them (SAS) or all three sides (SSS). With $C = 90^\circ$ it becomes the Pythagorean theorem.
Area of any triangle: $\frac12ab\sin C$, half the product of two sides and the sine of the angle between them.

example.s: Two sides and the included angle: Law of Cosines. $c^2 = 49+100-2(7)(10)\cos60^\circ = 149-70 = 79$, so $c = \sqrt{79}\approx8.89$.

pitfalls: Using the Law of Sines with SAS or SSS, where no side-angle pair is known.
Forgetting the second triangle in the ambiguous case.
SECTIONS.tip: Ask: do I know a side and its opposite angle? Yes, Law of Sines. No, Law of Cosines.

items.d: Quadrant I: all positive. II: sine. III: tangent. IV: cosine.
Sine and cosine 2π; tangent and cotangent π.
A side and its opposite angle known: Law of Sines. SAS or SSS: Law of Cosines.

exam1.title: Exam 1 practice
exam1.subtitle: Angles, right triangles and the unit circle. No calculator: give exact values and explain each step.

problems.q: Convert $225^\circ$ to radians and $\frac{7\pi}{6}$ to degrees.
A circle has radius 6 cm. Find the length of the arc cut off by a central angle of $40^\circ$, and the area of that sector.
A 6 ft person casts a 4 ft shadow while a flagpole casts a 22 ft shadow. How tall is the flagpole? Explain why your method works.
problems.s: The sun's rays make the same angle with both, so the triangles are similar and their sides proportional: $\frac{h}{22} = \frac64$, so $h = 33$ ft.

problems.q: From a point 40 m from the base of a building, the angle of elevation to its top is $60^\circ$. How tall is the building?

problems.s: $\frac{4\pi}3$: quadrant III, reference $\frac\pi3$: $-\frac{\sqrt3}2$. $\frac{3\pi}4$: quadrant II, reference $\frac\pi4$: $-\frac{\sqrt2}2$. $\frac{11\pi}6$: quadrant IV, reference $\frac\pi6$: $\tan = -\frac{1}{\sqrt3} = -\frac{\sqrt3}3$.

problems.q: If $\cos t = -\frac{5}{13}$ and $t$ is in quadrant III, find $\sin t$, $\tan t$ and $\csc t$.
problems.s: Reference triangle 5-12-13. In quadrant III sine is negative and tangent positive: $\sin t = -\frac{12}{13}$, $\tan t = \frac{12}{5}$, $\csc t = -\frac{13}{12}$.

problems.q: Use even/odd properties to find $\cos\left(-\frac\pi3\right)$ and $\sin\left(-\frac\pi4\right)$.
problems.s: Cosine is even: $\cos\frac\pi3 = \frac12$. Sine is odd: $-\sin\frac\pi4 = -\frac{\sqrt2}2$.

problems.q: If $\sin t = 0.6$ and $\cos t\lt0$, find $\cos t$ using $\sin^2t+\cos^2t = 1$.

exam2.title: Exam 2 practice
exam2.subtitle: Graphs, inverses, identities and the triangle laws. No calculator: exact answers, with each step explained.

problems.q: For $y = -2\sin\left(3x-\pi\right)+1$, find the amplitude, period, phase shift, midline and range.
problems.s: Rewrite as $-2\sin\big(3(x-\frac\pi3)\big)+1$. Amplitude 2, period $\frac{2\pi}3$, phase shift $\frac\pi3$ right, midline $y = 1$, range $[-1, 3]$.
The angle has adjacent 2, hypotenuse 3, so opposite $\sqrt{9-4} = \sqrt5$. It is in $[0,\frac\pi2]$, so $\tan = \frac{\sqrt5}2$.
$\cos x = -\frac12$: reference angle $\frac\pi3$, cosine negative in II and III: $x = \frac{2\pi}3, \frac{4\pi}3$.
Multiply the left side by $\frac{1+\cos x}{1+\cos x}$: $\frac{\sin x(1+\cos x)}{1-\cos^2x} = \frac{\sin x(1+\cos x)}{\sin^2x} = \frac{1+\cos x}{\sin x}$.

problems.q: If $\sin\theta = \frac45$ with $\theta$ in quadrant II, find $\sin2\theta$ and $\cos2\theta$.
(a) A triangle has $A = 30^\circ$, $B = 45^\circ$ and $a = 10$. Find $b$. (b) A triangle has sides 5, 7 and 8. Find the angle opposite the side of length 7.
problems.s: (a) Law of Sines: $b = \frac{10\sin45^\circ}{\sin30^\circ} = \frac{10\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}2}{\frac12} = 10\sqrt2\approx14.1$. (b) Law of Cosines: $49 = 25+64-80\cos B$, so $\cos B = \frac{40}{80} = \frac12$ and $B = 60^\circ$.

exam1: I can convert between degrees and radians and find coterminal angles.
I can find arc length and sector area with the angle in radians.
I can use SOH CAH TOA, the special triangles and similar triangles to find sides and heights.
I can write the first quadrant of the unit circle from memory.
I can find sine, cosine and tangent of any special angle using reference angles and signs.
I can find all six trig values from one value and the quadrant.
I can use even/odd properties and the Pythagorean identities.
exam2: I can find the amplitude, period, phase shift and midline of a sinusoid and sketch it.
I can describe why sine is odd and cosine is even from their graphs.
I can evaluate inverse trig functions within their ranges and simplify compositions with triangles.
I can solve basic trig equations on [0, 2π).
I can verify identities by working one side.
I can use the sum, difference and double-angle formulas for exact values.
I can choose and apply the Law of Sines or Cosines, and find a triangle’s area.

INFO.title: Homework and quizzes
INFO.html:
• WeBWorK: an assignment for each section, generally due Mondays at 8:00 pm. No late work, since solutions post right away. Start early.
  • Written homework: weekly, to the M170 folder in Gradescope. You may work together and ask for help, but submit your own work. 8 of 12 points are for attempting every part; 4 are for one question graded on the math you show. Solutions go up in Canvas Modules afterwards: use them to study.
  • Quizzes: in class; no make-ups without an approved absence arranged beforehand. Your lowest quiz score(s) are dropped.

INFO.title: Written work
INFO.html: Show all your work, explain it in words as well as equations, use correct notation, and don’t hand in scratch paper. Equations without explanation do not get full credit, and answers alone get little or none. Each item is scored 4 (complete), 3 (substantial), 2 (developing), 1 (minimal) or 0 (not seriously attempted); the rubric is on the Grade calculator page.

INFO.title: AI and academic integrity
INFO.html:
• AI is allowed as a support tool for learning, such as clarifying concepts, practice questions, checking your work or study plans, but not to replace your own thinking, problem solving or written work.
  • The syllabus’s best practices: attempt the problem first, ask specific questions, and verify every result yourself.
  • Answers from solution manuals or Q&A sites count as cheating unless allowed; acknowledge collaborators and cite sources.
  • Mathub fits the policy when you use it to practise and to check your understanding.

INFO.title: How to use Mathub for this class
INFO.html: Learn the unit circle first: run its flashcards until you can write the first quadrant from memory and get the others by symmetry. After each Wednesday class, read that topic’s notes and do a few quizzer questions before the Monday WeBWorK. Exams are by hand with no calculator, so do the practice sets on paper and explain every step.

QUIZ.hint: Draw a picture: a unit circle, a reference triangle or the triangle you are solving.

angles: Degrees to radians: × π/180. Radians to degrees: × 180/π.
Arc length s = rθ needs θ in radians.
righttri: Label opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse from the angle you are using.
unitcircle: Find the quadrant and the reference angle.
Use the first-quadrant value of the reference angle.
Attach the sign: All Students Take Calculus.
otherfns: Write it in sines and cosines.
Draw the reference triangle; find the missing side.
graphs: Write it as A sin(B(x − C)) + D.
Phase shift C: factor B out first.
inverse: Pick the one angle in that range.
For compositions, draw the triangle for the inner angle.
identities: Use sin² + cos² = 1 and common denominators.
sumdiff: Split the angle into special angles (45 ± 30, 60 ± 45).
Sine keeps the sign; cosine flips it.
Double angle: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ.
laws: Do you know a side and its opposite angle? Law of Sines.
SAS or SSS? Law of Cosines.
